name: Nitric acid in medieval Latin alchemy
summary: Alchemists writing in Latin around 1300 gave the earliest clear description of nitric acid, which dissolves most metals and separates silver from gold.
description: The Pseudo-Geber alchemical corpus, originating around 1300, contains the earliest clearly identifiable description of nitric acid, a corrosive mineral acid that dissolves all metals except gold and so can part silver from gold. The acid went under several names in alchemists' laboratories before the term aqua fortis appeared in the early fifteenth century, and within a century craftspeople were using it for practical work. Claims of earlier Islamic descriptions are disputed and are left open, as are the dates of sulfuric and hydrochloric acid.

impact.note: Scored on the general view, with the cited paper supporting the uses and the later transmission to China: the acids were the working reagents of a few trades, alchemists, assayers, metalworkers and etchers, across several societies (reach 1), gave a new capability to dissolve metals and part gold from silver (depth 2), and chemistry, assaying, etching and later the explosives, dye and fertiliser industries came to rest on them (generativity 3).

date.label: c. 1300 CE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: The earliest clearly identifiable description of nitric acid is in the Pseudo-Geber corpus, originating around 1300.

evidence.supports: The earliest clearly identifiable description can be found in the socalled Pseudo-Geber corpus originating around 1300
evidence.locator: Section 1, 'Prologue: Aqua fortis in Renaissance Europe', pp. 50–51

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Assess the Al-Hassan claim that pre-13th-century Islamic texts describe nitric acid, from primary Arabic manuscripts or a peer-reviewed study.
Date aqua regia and hydrochloric acid separately, and date sulfuric acid's earliest preparation (Karpenko and Norris on vitriol).
Confirm the Pseudo-Geber dating, the text concerned and its place of writing from a study of the corpus itself; the paper cited is about China and mentions it in passing.

research.note: Cao (2024) calls the Pseudo-Geber description the earliest clearly identifiable one; a claim of earlier Islamic descriptions (Al-Hassan) is disputed and was not settled by any source opened.
